prime.problem: A Dynamo-style store calls a write done after w of n replicas ack and a read done after r answer. Pick w and r too small and reads can miss the latest write; too large and every request waits on slow replicas. "Eventually consistent" gives no number to choose with: how often is a read stale, and for how long?
prime.fits: Builds on the eventual-consistency card (replicas accept writes alone) and the service-discovery card's majority quorums. This card generalises the overlap to any w and r, and turns "eventual" into a probability. Raft, next, uses the w = r = majority case with a leader.
expect: w + r > n: read and write sets overlap
WARS: write, ack, read, response latencies
LWW, read repair and Riak's corner cases
prime.goal: Explain why w + r > n makes the newest value appear among a read's answers, compute how often a partial quorum reads stale, and say why overlap still isn't a guarantee of fresh reads.

attend: Why must 3 + 3 picks among 5 replicas land on some replica twice, and what does that replica guarantee the read?
With n = 3, w = 1, r = 1, why is a read right at the ack stale 2/3 of the time?
Why did the WARS simulation measure only 0.486 stale at t = 0, below the 2/3 bound?
Why is replication lag easy to measure with a leader and undefined for a leaderless store?
Overlap puts the newest value in the answers. What can still make the store return an old one?

must: Write waits for w acks, read for r answers → if w + r > n the two sets share ≥ w + r − n replicas (pigeonhole) → at least one answer has the latest acked write → the read can pick it

w + r ≤ n (a partial quorum) → the read set can miss every replica holding the new value → P(stale) = C(n − k, r)/C(n, r) with k replicas holding it → 2/3 at the ack for n = 3, w = r = 1 → "eventual" becomes a number
The write keeps spreading after the ack → the longer the read waits (t), the more replicas have it → WARS: fresh 0.514 at t = 0 rising to 0.959 at 50 ms → staleness is both how often and for how long

Overlap delivers the newest value but the store must still know which is newest → with last-write-wins and skewed clocks it can pick the older one; a partly failed write can be spread by read repair → w + r > n is not linearizability
elevated: Each tuning point trades staleness for latency and availability → w tolerates n − w failures for writes, r tolerates n − r for reads → Riak-style w = r = 1 stays writable when most replicas are down, at the price the table quantifies
reference: Riak's PW/PR options and their corner case
WARS's latency distributions (exponential, means 20 and 5 ms) and 100,000 trials
the Bailis et al. PBS paper naming

compress.prompt: From memory, write the overlap inequality, the staleness formula and the k-staleness formula, each with one worked number. Then one sentence on why overlap still isn't a freshness guarantee.
checklist: w + r > n → overlap ≥ w + r − n ≥ 1 replica
P(stale) = C(n − k, r)/C(n, r): 2/3 for n = 3, k = 1, r = 1
within the last j versions: 1 − P<sup>j</sup> (0.556 at j = 2)
waiting helps: WARS fresh 0.514 → 0.959 over 50 ms
LWW with clock skew and read repair of failed writes still return old or unexpected values
stronger promises need transactions or consensus

retrieve.q: Explain why a partial quorum (w + r ≤ n) can be the right choice, and what number you should compute before choosing it.
answer: it's faster (waits for fewer replicas) and stays writable/readable with more replicas down
the price is a nonzero chance of stale reads
compute P(stale) at the ack and how quickly it falls with time (PBS/WARS), then decide if the app can live with it

retrieve.q: Walk through the source's Figure 1 with R4 and R5 down, then the all-up contrast where the read asks R3, R4, R5: what does each read return and why?
answer: down case: the write lands on R1–R3 (w = 3); the read can only ask R1–R3, all answer v2
all-up case: the write was acked by R1–R3, the read asks R3, R4, R5 → v2, v1, v1
R3 is the overlap, so the newest version v2 is among the answers and wins
read repair then writes v2 back to R4 and R5

retrieve.q: Why is the table's 2/3 an upper bound on staleness for a read issued right at the ack, and what makes real systems fresher still?
answer: at the ack at least k = w replicas have the value; more may already have it
while the ack and read travel, the write keeps spreading (WARS measured 0.486 stale, not 0.667)
read repair and anti-entropy, left out of WARS, spread it further

compare.q: Raft commits on a majority and reads through the leader; a Dynamo-style store with w = r = 2 of 3 also overlaps. What does Raft's leader add that the quorum store lacks, and what does the quorum store keep that Raft gives up?
answer: Raft's leader puts all writes in one order, so there's no "which version is newest" question and no LWW clock skew
the quorum store has no leader to fail over: any replica can take writes, so it stays available with more combinations of failures
Raft refuses writes without a majority; a partial-quorum store keeps accepting them at a quantified staleness

compare.q: The staleness formula is a hypergeometric count. Map its parts onto the capture-recapture setting: what are the "marked" items, the population and the sample?
answer: population: the n replicas; marked: the k that already have the new value
the sample: the r replicas the read hears from, drawn without replacement
P(stale) is the chance the sample contains zero marked items: C(n − k, r)/C(n, r)

predict.q: A 5-replica store uses w = 2, r = 2. Right at the ack (k = 2), what is P(stale)? And what is the chance a read returns one of the last two versions? Commit first.
predict.answer: w + r = 4 ≤ 5, so staleness is possible. P(stale) = C(3, 2)/C(5, 2) = 3/10. Within the last 2 versions: 1 − (3/10)<sup>2</sup> = 0.91. For comparison, n = 5 with w = r = 1 is stale 4/5 at the ack, and w = 3, r = 2 is stale 1/10 even though it still doesn't overlap.

apply.task: Using p_stale from code/quorums-staleness.py, fill in a table for n = 5: rows r = 1, 2, 3, columns k = 1…5. Mark the cells where w + r > n would hold with w = k. Then run the WARS simulation for n = 5 with (w, r) = (1, 1) and (3, 3) at t = 0 and 20 ms, and compare the measured staleness with the table's bound.
apply.done: Your n = 5 table has 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5, 0 in the r = 1 row and zeros exactly where k + r > 5; wars(5, 3, 3, [0, 20]) gives 1.0 fresh at both times; wars(5, 1, 1, [0, 20]) gives 0.385 and 0.774, fresher than the table's 1 − 4/5 = 0.2 at the ack, and you can say why.
apply.hint: r = 2 row: C(5−k, 2)/10 = 6/10, 3/10, 1/10, 0, 0. r = 3 row: C(5−k, 3)/10 = 4/10, 1/10, 0, 0, 0. The simulation's fresher-than-bound result has the same cause as n = 3: the write keeps spreading during the read.
